{{Short description|Theoretical physicist (born 1941)}}

Ta-Pei Cheng (Chinese: 鄭大培; born 1941) is a [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] and professor emeritus of physics at the [[University of Missouri–St. Louis]].<ref name="IAS Profile">{{cite web
 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/ta-pei-cheng
 |title=Ta-Pei Cheng IAS Scholar Profile
 |website=Institute for Advanced Study
 |date=December 9, 2019
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref><ref name="UMSL Physics">{{cite web
|url=https://bulletin.umsl.edu/artsandsciences/mathematics-physics-astronomy-and-statistics/#faculty
 |title=UMSL Physics Faculty
 |website=University of Missouri-St. Louis
 |date=n.d.
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref><ref name="IASComScholar">{{cite report
 |title=A Community of Scholars: The Institute for Advanced Study, Faculty and Members 1930-1980
 |publisher=The Institute for Advanced Study
 |date=1980
|url=https://www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/library/pdfs/hs/cos.pdf
 |format=PDF
 |page=117
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref> Cheng’s research has included work on low-energy theorem relating the [[Nucleon spin structure|nucleon sigma term]] to the [[pion]]-nucleon scattering amplitude at the Cheng–[[Roger Dashen|Dashen]] point,<ref name="Alarcón">{{cite journal
|last=Alarcón
|first=J. M.
|title=Brief history of the pion–nucleon sigma term
|journal=The European Physical Journal Special Topics
|year=2021
|volume=230
|issue=6
|pages=1609–1622
|doi=10.1140/epjs/s11734-021-00145-6
}}</ref> and studies with [[Estia Eichten]] and [[Ling-Fong Li]] of [[asymptotic freedom]] and [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]] in [[Gauge theory|gauge theories]].<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Cheng
|first1=T. P.
|last2=Eichten
|first2=E.
|last3=Li
|first3=Ling-Fong
|title=Higgs phenomena in asymptotically free gauge theories
|journal=Physical Review D
|year=1974
|volume=9
|issue=8
|pages=2259–2273
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.9.2259
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Marciano
|first1=William
|last2=Pagels
|first2=Heinz
|title=Quantum chromodynamics
|journal=Physics Reports
|year=1978
|volume=36
|issue=3
|page=199
|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(78)90208-9
}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1982.<ref name="IAS Profile"/>

==Early life and education==
Cheng was born in [[Shanghai]] in 1941 and spent part of his childhood in [[Qingdao]].<ref name="IASComScholar"/><ref name="biography">{{cite web
 |last=Cheng
 |first=Ta-Pei
 |title=Biography
|url=https://www.tapeicheng.com/biography
 |website=TaPeiCheng.com
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref> In 1956, during the [[Hundred Flowers]] period, he moved to [[Hong Kong]] to join his parents.<ref name="biography"/> After completing secondary school in Hong Kong, he moved to the United States to study at [[Dartmouth College]], where he received an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] degree in 1964.<ref name="IASComScholar"/><ref name="biography"/> He then pursued graduate study in theoretical physics at [[Rockefeller University]] in New York City, working under the particle physicist and Einstein biographer [[Abraham Pais]] and completing his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1969.<ref name="IASComScholar"/><ref>{{cite thesis
 |last=Cheng
 |first=Ta-Pei
 |title=Radiative Corrections to Low Energy Theorems
 |degree=PhD
 |publisher=The Rockefeller University
 |year=1969
|url=https://digitalcommons.rockefeller.edu/student_theses_and_dissertations/558/
 |doi=10.48496/1byd-9z15
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref>
==Academic career==
Cheng was a postdoctoral member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (IAS) in Princeton, New Jersey.<ref name="IAS Profile"/><ref name="IASComScholar"/> He then returned to Rockefeller University as a research associate from 1971 to 1973.<ref name="IAS Profile"/>

In 1973 Cheng joined the faculty of the [[University of Missouri–St. Louis]] (UMSL) as an assistant professor of physics.<ref name="IAS Profile"/> He was promoted to associate professor in 1976 and to full professor in 1978.<ref name="IAS Profile"/> He served as chair of the Department of Physics at UMSL from 1978 to 1979.<ref name="IAS Profile"/> He retired from full-time teaching in 2007 and was named professor emeritus.<ref name="IAS Profile"/><ref name="UMSL Physics"/>

Cheng held visiting positions from 1977–1978 at the Institute for Advanced Study, from 1979–1980 at the [[University of Minnesota]], from 1982–1983 at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory]], from 1987–1988 at IAS, and from 1991–1992 at the [[Chinese University of Hong Kong]].<ref name="IAS Profile"/><ref>{{cite book
 |last=Cheng
 |first=Ta-Pei
 |title=Einstein's Physics: Atoms, Quanta, and Relativity - Derived, Explained, and Appraised
 |publisher=Oxford University Press
 |year=2013
 |isbn=978-0-19-966991-2
 |at=Dust jacket
}}</ref><ref name="ChengCV">{{cite web
 |last=Cheng
 |first=Ta-Pei
 |title=Curriculum Vitae
|url=https://www.tapeicheng.com/curriculum-vitae
 |website=Ta-Pei Cheng
 |access-date=August 19, 2026
}}</ref> He also made extended research visits to the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], [[CERN]], [[Fermilab]], and the [[Aspen Center for Physics]].<ref name="biography"/><ref name="ChengLiBook">{{cite book
 |last1=Cheng
 |first1=Ta-Pei
 |last2=Li
 |first2=Ling-Fong
 |title=Gauge Theory of Elementary Particle Physics
 |location=Oxford
 |publisher=Clarendon Press
 |year=1984
 |page=vi
 |isbn=978-0-19-851961-4
}}</ref> From 2002 to 2008, Cheng was an honorary professor of physics at the [[University of Hong Kong]].<ref>{{cite web
|last=Cheng
|first=Ta-Pei
|title=Curriculum Vitae
|url=https://www.umsl.edu/~chengt/Vita2015.pdf
|website=University of Missouri–St. Louis
|format=PDF
|access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref> Beginning in 2009, he also served as an adjunct professor of physics at [[Portland State University]].<ref>{{cite web
|last=Cheng
|first=Ta-Pei
|title=Curriculum Vitae
|url=https://www.umsl.edu/~chengt/Vita2010.pdf
|website=University of Missouri–St. Louis
|format=PDF
|access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine
|title=New Works
|magazine=Portland State Magazine
|publisher=Portland State University
|date=Spring 2013
|page=9
|url=https://content.library.pdx.edu/files/PDXScholar/Portland-State-Magazine-Spring-2013/11/
|access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref>

==Research==
Cheng’s research has focused on theoretical [[particle physics]], including [[Gauge theory|gauge theories]] and the quark structure of the nucleon.<ref name="IASComScholar"/><ref name="Gross"/><ref name="ChengCV"/> Early in his career, Cheng studied low-energy theorems and [[chiral symmetry]].<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Cheng
|first1=T. P.
|last2=Dashen
|first2=Roger F.
|title=Is SU(2)×SU(2) a Better Symmetry than SU(3)?
|journal=Physical Review Letters
|year=1971
|volume=26
|issue=10
|pages=594–597
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.26.594
}}</ref> With [[Roger Dashen]], he derived a relation connecting the low-energy [[pion]]–[[nucleon]] scattering amplitude at what became known as the Cheng–Dashen point to the nucleon sigma term.<ref name="IASComScholar"/><ref name="Alarcón"/>

He undertook a systematic study, with [[Estia Eichten|Eichten]] and [[Ling-Fong Li|Li]], of the [[Renormalization group|renormalization group]] structure of gauge theories with [[Higgs mechanism|Higgs fields]].<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Cheng
|first1=T. P.
|last2=Eichten
|first2=E.
|last3=Li
|first3=Ling-Fong
|title=Higgs phenomena in asymptotically free gauge theories
|journal=Physical Review D
|year=1974
|volume=9
|issue=8
|pages=2259–2273
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.9.2259
}}</ref> Cheng, Eichten, and Li found that, in the classes of gauge theories they examined, [[asymptotic freedom]] could not coexist with complete breaking of the gauge symmetry through the Higgs mechanism.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Marciano
 |first1=William
 |last2=Pagels
 |first2=Heinz
 |title=Quantum chromodynamics
 |journal=Physics Reports
 |year=1978
 |volume=36
 |issue=3
 |page=199
 |doi=10.1016/0370-1573(78)90208-9
}}</ref> The work was cited by [[Howard Georgi|Georgi]] and [[Sheldon Glashow|Glashow]] in their 1974 paper proposing [[Georgi–Glashow model|SU(5) grand unification]].<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Georgi
 |first1=Howard
 |last2=Glashow
 |first2=S. L.
 |title=Unity of All Elementary-Particle Forces
 |journal=Physical Review Letters
 |year=1974
 |volume=32
 |issue=8
 |page=439
 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.438
}}</ref> Cheng and Li also worked on [[Neutrino mass|neutrino masses]] and related [[Flavour (particle physics)|lepton-flavor]] nonconservation effects.<ref name="IASComScholar"/>

A 2021 [[Stanford University]] bibliometric analysis ranked Cheng among the top 2% of researchers in his field for career-long citation impact.<ref>{{cite web
 |last=Walentik
 |first=Steve
 |title=UMSL faculty members ranked among the top 2% of scholars worldwide
|url=https://blogs.umsl.edu/news/2022/03/16/faculty-members-ranked-among-the-top-scholars-worldwide/
 |website=UMSL Daily
 |publisher=University of Missouri–St. Louis
 |date=March 16, 2022
 |access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref> As of August 2026, [[Google Scholar]] listed more than 10,000 citations to Cheng's publications.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=Ta-Pei Cheng
|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ow_m0PYAAAAJ&hl=en
 |website=Google Scholar
 |access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref> In 1982, Cheng was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="IAS Profile"/>

==Textbooks and popular works==
Cheng is the co-author, with [[Ling-Fong Li]], of ''Gauge Theory of Elementary Particle Physics'', a graduate-level text on gauge field theories and the [[Standard Model]] published by [[Oxford University Press]].<ref name="Gross"/><ref name="ChengLiBook"/> The book has remained in use as a graduate-level reference in particle physics and quantum field theory,<ref name="Gross"/><ref>{{cite web
 |title=The Standard Model
|url=https://edu.epfl.ch/coursebook/en/the-standard-model-PHYS-505
 |website=EPFL Coursebook
 |publisher=École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne
 |access-date=August 20, 2026
}}</ref> and Oxford University Press later described it as a well-established textbook in the field.<ref name="Oxford 2000"/>

He later turned his attention to [[general relativity]] and [[cosmology]], authoring ''Relativity, Gravitation and Cosmology: A Basic Introduction'', published in the Oxford Master Series in Physics.<ref name="Hamilton"/> The book appeared in a second edition in 2010<ref>{{cite book
|last=Cheng
|first=Ta-Pei
|title=Relativity, Gravitation and Cosmology: A Basic Introduction
|edition=2nd
|publisher=Oxford University Press
|year=2010
|isbn=978-0-19-957363-9
|doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199573639.001.0001
}}</ref> and was reviewed in journals including the ''American Journal of Physics''<ref name="Hamilton"/> and ''General Relativity and Gravitation''.<ref name="Nolan"/>

Cheng has also written ''Einstein’s Physics: Atoms, Quanta, and Relativity — Derived, Explained, and Appraised'', which presents Einstein’s contributions to physics in a historical and conceptual framework for advanced undergraduates and general readers with a physics background.<ref name="Hubisz"/><ref name="Rafelski"/> He later wrote ''A College Course on Relativity and Cosmology'', intended for upper-level undergraduate students in physics and astronomy.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Cheng
 |first=Ta-Pei
 |title=A College Course on Relativity and Cosmology
 |chapter=Preface
 |publisher=Oxford University Press
 |year=2015
 |pages=vii–viii
 |isbn=978-0-19-969340-5
 |doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199693405.002.0005
}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He is married to Leslie Su Cheng and has three children.<ref name="biography"/>
